sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains the apparent redundancy of the word "leimor" in the verse, and introduces two interpretations regarding the innovation of the Giving of the Torah.

translations.translation: “And Elokim spoke all these words, saying,”
And the precise point is known
regarding what is written “saying,”
that since all of Israel
(the souls of all generations)
were present at Mount Sinai and heard the Ten Commandments from the Holy One, blessed be He, Himself,
what is the meaning of “saying”?
It means “to say to others.”
And the point of the explanation in this is,
that through this the verse explains the innovation of the Giving of the Torah.
For seemingly, even before the Giving of the Torah they studied the entire Torah
[as is also understood from the fact that Avraham Avinu fulfilled the entire Torah before it was given,
for in order to fulfill the Torah one must study it,
and certainly
Avraham taught the entire Torah to his son Yitzchak, and Yitzchak taught it to Yaakov and his sons],
and what is the innovation of the Giving of the Torah?
And the verse explains,
that the innovation of “And Elokim spoke all these words” at the Giving of the Torah is,
that through this the power was given to each and every Jew of all generations,
that his study of Torah should be in a manner of “saying.”
And there are two explanations in this.
That through his study of Torah he causes the Holy One, blessed be He, to speak these words,
for whoever reads and reviews, the Holy One, blessed be He, reads and reviews opposite him,
according to which the explanation of “saying”
(“to say to others”)
is,
that the person who studies Torah says to the Holy One, blessed be He,
as it were, that He should repeat his words.
And furthermore,
that a person’s study of Torah should be in a manner of “saying,”
to repeat the words that the Holy One, blessed be He, says,
as it is written,
“May my tongue answer Your word,”
that the words of Torah that a person says are “Your word,” and “my tongue answers” like one who answers after the reader.
And there is another explanation of “And [He] spoke… saying,”
that “And Elokim spoke all these words,”
the Ten Commandments which are the general principles of the entire Torah,
is “saying,”
that the Ten Commandments
(Torah that is above the world)
should be drawn down into the Ten Utterances through which
the world was created.
And likewise is it in a person’s study of Torah,
that it is in a manner of “And [He] spoke… saying,”
that from his Torah speech an “utterance” is made,
the drawing down of influence below.
And one must understand the connection and relevance of all the above matters in “saying.”

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section cites the Mitteler Rebbe's maamar and the Midrash, explaining that the voice at Sinai was tailored to each individual's capacity, including the physical body.

translations.translation: Now, in the maamar of the Mitteler Rebbe beginning with this verse, which was said one hundred years ago,
(after the precise point that the word “leimor” seems superfluous),
he brings what is stated in the Yalkut,
“When the Holy One, blessed be He, was speaking, each Jew would say, ‘The speech speaks with me,’ as it is stated,
‘I am the L‑rd your G‑d’ in the singular.”
And he explains,
that this is what is stated in the Midrash
on the verse “I am the L‑rd your G‑d,”
that the voice they heard at the Ten Commandments was according to the capacity of each individual,
the youths according to their capacity, the elders according to their capacity, and the children according to their capacity.
And it can be said,
that from the reasons for this that he also brings from the statement of the Midrash,
it is,
that through this it is understood that the matter of “the speech speaks with me”
(to each one individually)
is not only in regard to the soul but also in regard to the body,
for the distinction of youths, elders, and children is from the aspect of the body.
